headline: Race at 5.8 Knots: Bass Come Wire-Line, First Bonito Scouts at Valiant
subhead: A brutal full-moon current is compressing every bite into a narrow slack window — but that window is producing quality fish, and the first bonito are finally showing at the Race.
body_markdown:
Five point eight knots. That's what the max ebb ran through the Race on Tuesday's peak tide, forty-eight hours off the full moon, and it's the number that dictated everything I did on the water this week. When the Race is moving that hard, you don't fish it — you fish the ten or twelve minutes on either side of the turn, and you'd better know exactly when that turn is coming. At Valiant Rock this week that window has been running roughly six hours off the New London low, and it's been shrinking, not growing, as we push through this moon cycle. Miss it by fifteen minutes and you're not fishing anymore, you're just holding on.

Inside that window, though, the bass have been solid. Wire line has been the difference-maker — 30-foot drops of single-strand behind bunker spoons and small umbrella rigs, worked over the rockpile in 45 to 65 feet on the last hour of ebb sliding into slack. Once the current eases enough to hold bottom contact, I've been switching guys over to 2-ounce bucktails dressed with white pork rind, dropped tight to the rock and swept with the dying current rather than ripped against it. That subtlety matters right now — New London's reading 69.8 degrees, a solid five degrees cooler than the water sitting up around Kings Point, and that thermal edge is exactly why the bass are stacking on the eastern structure instead of spreading out through the open Sound. Cooler water, hard current, standing rock — that's the recipe, and Valiant and Race Rock have both been holding up their end.

The honest part of this report is that it's not an all-day bite. Outside that slack window, the current is simply too strong to present anything cleanly, and the fish know it — they tuck into the eddies behind the rock and wait it out just like we do. I've had trips where we boated four keeper bass in twenty minutes of slack and then spent the next three hours getting nothing but arm-tired from bucktails skipping off bottom in five knots of push. If you're planning a trip to the Race or Plum Gut this week, build your whole day around that turn. Everything else is just positioning.

Plum Gut itself has been the better bet for fluke over the bass grounds proper. The channel edges on the west side, where the bottom drops from 20 feet down into the 35-to-40-foot cut, have been holding doormats on the tide change — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow with the last of the current before it goes dead. The full-moon tide swing has sharpened that drift bite noticeably; bigger water movement means more bait getting swept off the flats and funneled through the Gut, and the fluke know exactly where to sit and wait for it.

Now for the fish everybody's been asking about. We flagged it last week — said bonito would show at the Race and the Fishers Island Sound corridor within days as temps closed in on that low-70s threshold, and here they are. Small scouting pods, nothing you'd call consistent yet, working bait pushed against the rip line off Little Gull and Great Gull Island. Epoxy jigs — half-ounce Deadly Dicks and Albie Snax in the smaller sizes — on 20-pound fluoro have drawn a handful of strikes on the edges of the current where it's calm enough to see the nervous water. This is not yet a fishery you plan a trip around. It's a fishery you keep gear rigged for while you're doing something else, because when it turns on in this corridor it turns on fast, and next week could be the week it does.

Black sea bass have stayed dependable and unglamorous, which is exactly what you want from them in August. The rockpile structure around Race Rock and the reef edges toward the Sluiceway are holding fish in that 50-to-70-foot range, right around where the thermocline sits this time of year. Diamond jigs tipped with squid, bounced tight to structure on the drift, have been steady without being spectacular — a good backup plan on days when the main current window doesn't cooperate or the wind kills your bonito scouting.

Bluefish have been mixed into the bass activity rather than running their own show — expect that to hold as bunker schools continue pushing through the Gut on their late-summer track. If you're wire-lining for bass and get bit off, don't be surprised if it's a blue instead; they're keying on the same bait right now.

Looking ahead, the moon's strength starts easing over the next several days, which should stretch those slack windows back out to something more forgiving — good news for anyone who's been getting squeezed by these five-plus-knot tides. I'd expect the bonito numbers at the Race and Fishers Island Sound to build through the back half of this week as the current calms and the water holds in that low-70s band. If I had one trip to make, I'd fish the Valiant Rock slack at first light for bass, then run out to the Gull Islands with epoxy jigs rigged and ready the moment the current lays down enough to see fish working.
